column4: The blind visitor may remember and the reminder may benefit him: this directly restages the source section's ذ ك ر and ن ف ع pairing.
The man who comes is described as وَهُوَ يَخْشَىٰ, matching the source section's one who receives the reminder through fear.
The Prophet is told he is distracted from the man; this is the same encounter's rejected attentiveness, set against 87:10's receiver.
The question وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ introduces the possibility that the visitor will purify himself, echoing 87:14 and the section's connection between fear and knowledge.
The one who comes striving is the same visitor whose approach the section contrasts with turning away from the reminder.
The Prophet's frown and turning away open the scene the section uses to show that a receptive listener may be passed over.
This ayah identifies the blind man's arrival; it completes 80:1's turning-away scene that the section explicitly invokes.
The man who considers himself self-sufficient is contrasted with the fearful visitor who comes seeking reminder in 80:8–9.
The Prophet is directed toward the self-sufficient man, completing the contrast with the fearful visitor in 80:8–10.
The Prophet is not accountable if the self-sufficient man does not purify himself, contrasting worldly standing with receptive fear.
إِنَّهَا تَذْكِرَةٌ calls the revelation a reminder, the same act named by the source root ذ ك ر.
فَمَن شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ makes the listener's taking up the reminder a matter of response, as in 87:10–11.
The command to remind is followed by the claim that the reminder benefits believers, directly echoing the source section's ذ ك ر and ن ف ع.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Qur'an whoever fears God's warning, joining the section's reminder, fearful recipient, and preacher's role.
The Prophet's task is explicitly to remind; this states the limited role behind the source section's command فَذَكِّرْ.
The Prophet is not a controller over his hearers; this boundary clarifies why the section distinguishes giving a reminder from forcing its acceptance.
The one who turns back and disbelieves is a direct counterpart to the source section's al-ashqa who keeps the reminder at a distance.
This ayah gives the punishment for the turner in 88:23, completing the consequence of avoiding the reminder that 87:11–13 places nearby in its own surah.
The Qur'an is a reminder for مَن يَخْشَىٰ, directly bringing together reminder and the fearful recipient as 87:9–10 do.
This says the Qur'an was not sent to distress the Prophet; it supplies the non-burdensome boundary immediately before 20:3's reminder for the fearful.
Moses and Aaron must speak gently to Pharaoh in hope that he remembers or fears, a direct parallel to offering reminder to a hearer who may respond.
Moses invites Pharaoh to purify himself, echoing both the possible purification in 80:3 and the success of 87:14.
Moses offers guidance to the Lord so Pharaoh may fear; this joins the source's secondary خشية-as-knowing gloss to the root ه د ي named in that gloss.
The great sign shown to Pharaoh is the message's concrete presentation; 79:21 then records his response, completing the invitation scene developed in the source.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys after the sign, showing the refused response opposite the fearful hearer in 87:10.
Pharaoh turns away and strives after refusing the sign, making the source's act of keeping the reminder at a distance explicit.
Pharaoh gathers his people and calls out; this continues his refusal in 79:21–22 and makes the audience to his counter-message visible.
Pharaoh claims to be their highest lord, the arrogant stance that answers Moses' invitation to turn toward the Lord in 79:19.
The seizure is the consequence of Pharaoh's denial and turning away in 79:21–24, completing the refusal scene.
The account is called a lesson for one who fears, explicitly linking the Pharaoh episode to the source section's fearful recipient.
This ayah joins warning to those who fear their Lord unseen, establish prayer, and purify themselves; it gathers the source's 87:10, 14, and 15 links.
It says those with knowledge fear Allah, directly supporting the source's gloss that خشية usually arises from knowledge.
The warning reaches one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, a precise statement of the source's receptive audience.
The signs benefit the one who sees and harm the one who is blind, while the Prophet is no guardian; this concretizes the source's benefit/harm distinction and limited role.
The Prophet is told to warn those who fear being gathered to their Lord, directly matching the source's fearful audience.
He must not drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening; this echoes the blind, seeking visitor in 80 and the source's received reminder.
The disbelievers question the worth of the humble believers in 6:52; this completes the status contrast that the source's 80 scene exposes.
The Prophet is told not to let his eyes pass beyond those invoking God while seeking the world's adornment; it closely parallels the warning against overlooking the fearful visitor in 80.
The one reminded of God's signs turns away and forgets what he sent ahead, a direct instance of the source's avoided reminder.
It asks who is more unjust than one reminded of God's signs who then turns away, directly formulating the source's second response.
The ayah asks why people turn away from the reminder, naming the same avoidant act described by the source's ج ن ب root.
The fleeing wild asses picture the people who turn away in 74:49; the image makes avoidance of reminder visible, while the source describes a quieter distancing.
The asses flee from a lion, completing 74:50's image for the people turning away from reminder in 74:49.
The ayah says they do not fear the Hereafter, the precise contrary of the fear through which 87:10's listener receives the reminder.
إِنَّهُۥ تَذْكِرَةٌ calls the message a reminder, directly echoing the source root ذ ك ر.
Whoever wills may remember, spelling out the voluntary response contrasted in 87:10–11.
It says they remember only if God wills and names Him أهل التقوى; this holds together the source's voluntary response and fear/awe theme.
The giver who fears God begins the positive path opposite the source's wretched avoider.
Belief in the best confirms the response begun in 92:5, supplying its faith commitment alongside fear.
God eases this person's way toward ease, echoing 87:8 and showing the outcome of the receptive, God-fearing path.
The one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient begins the negative path opposite 92:5 and the source's fearful listener.
He denies the best, explicitly showing the refusal paired with the source's one who avoids reminder.
The difficult way is made easy for the refuser of 92:8–9, completing the two paths set against each other.
His wealth cannot avail him when he falls, undercutting the worldly self-sufficiency opposed by the source's lasting hereafter.
إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ names guidance as God's charge, echoing the source's explicit ه د ي root link.
The first life and the Hereafter belong to God, framing the source's contrast between preferred worldly life and the better, enduring one.
The warning of a blazing fire is the announced consequence of rejecting the path, as in the surrounding 87:11–13 context.
The word الْأَشْقَى names the one entering the fire, matching the source's word for the wretched avoider.
The wretched one's defining acts are denial and turning away, explicitly aligning al-ashqa with the source's avoidance of reminder.
سَيُجَنَّبُهَا uses the source root ج ن ب for the God-fearing person kept away from the fire, reversing 87:11's wretched person who keeps away from reminder.
The God-fearing man gives wealth to purify himself, echoing the purification of 87:14.
He gives without repaying a favor owed to anyone, making his action unlike worldly calculation and self-sufficiency.
His giving seeks only his Lord's countenance, showing the motive behind the receptive, God-fearing path.
The giver will be satisfied, the good end set against the source's al-ashqa and its wretched consequence.
The Day divides people into شَقِيٌّ and سَعِيدٌ, explicitly spelling out the misery/happiness opposition named in the source root gloss.
The wretched are placed in the Fire, carrying the source's al-ashqa from 87:11 into the consequence stated in 87:12.
The wretched remain in the Fire through the appointed duration; this completes 11:106's fate and recalls 87:13's condition in the Fire.
The happy are in the Garden without end, completing 11:105's contrast and echoing 87:17's better, abiding Hereafter.
The criminal's Hell is described with لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ, the exact fate named just after the source image in 87:13.
The believer who does good receives high ranks, contrasting the wretched criminal of 20:74 and the source's successful purifier.
The gardens are the reward of one who purifies himself, joining the source's 87:14 purification to its contrast with fire.
Whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray nor be wretched, the opposite of the source's al-ashqa who avoids the reminder; the verse also uses the ه د ي root in its source gloss.
Whoever turns away from God's remembrance receives a constricted life, a direct statement of the consequence of the source's avoidance.
God says His signs came but were disregarded, so the person is disregarded that Day; this names the consequence of refusing the reminder.
The afterlife punishment is more severe and more enduring than the worldly one, echoing 87:17's better and abiding Hereafter.
The transgressor begins the path contrasted with the fearful recipient of reminder in the source section.
Preferring the worldly life states the choice condemned by 87:16 and opposed to the abiding Hereafter.
Hell is the transgressor's refuge, completing the worldly preference in 79:38 and the fire for 87:11's al-ashqa.
The one who fears standing before his Lord restrains desire, embodying the receptive fear and self-restraint contrasted with al-ashqa.
The Garden is the refuge for the one who fears and restrains himself, completing the contrast with 79:39 and 87:12–17.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا directly echoes 87:14's success for the one who purifies himself.
The one who corrupts the soul fails, completing 91:9's purification contrast and clarifying the source's al-ashqa.
The unbelievers' fire is not ended by death and their punishment is not lightened, a close counterpart to the source's fire and no-life/no-death context.
The damned say that a warner came and that they had time to remember, directly tying the punishment to refusing the offered reminder.
When God is mentioned the believers' hearts tremble and recited signs increase faith, a concrete positive response to reminder through fear.
Believers are commanded not to turn away from the Messenger while hearing him, the same act of turning aside that the source marks in the avoider.
The people who say they hear but do not hear expose the difference between receiving a reminder and merely encountering it.
The deaf and dumb who do not reason are called the worst creatures, a stark image of refusing what is heard.
Even if made to hear, they would turn away; the verse directly describes the source's avoidant response.
God and the Messenger call believers to what gives life, a boundary against the deadened refusal in 8:21–23 and the source's fire scene.
The people in the Fire admit a warner came and they denied him, directly connecting refusal of warning with the source's wretched outcome.
They say that listening or reasoning would have kept them from the Blaze, completing the admission in 67:9 and the source's contrast of hearers.
They acknowledge their sin in the Fire, completing 67:9–10's rejected warning and its consequence.
Those who fear their Lord unseen receive forgiveness and great reward, the positive counterpart to the deniers in 67:9–11 and to the source's listener.
When told اِتَّقِ اللَّهَ, the hearer grows proud and sins; this is a specific rejection of admonition to fear, ending in Hell.
Trade does not distract these people from God's ذكر, prayer, and fear of the Day, joining the source's remembered name, prayer, and worldly-life contrast.
At the call to Friday prayer, people must leave trade and hasten to remembrance, linking the source's prayer and remembrance against worldly distraction.
After prayer, people may seek God's provision while remembering Him much, showing how worldly provision can coexist with the remembrance the source contrasts with preference for dunya.
The congregation disperses toward trade and amusement, leaving the Prophet standing; this concretely stages worldly distraction from reminder and prayer.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembrance of Allah; those who do so are losers, echoing 87:16's worldly preference.
God commands worship and prayer لِذِكْرِي, directly joining the source's remembrance of the Lord's name and prayer in 87:15.
The recited Book and prayer are joined to God's ذكر, the same relation made explicit by 87:15 in the source section's discussion.
Believers' hearts are asked to humble to God's remembrance and revealed truth, contrasting receptivity with hardened distance from reminder.
Those who are apprehensive of their Lord's awe are identified as the first group in a portrait of receptive believers.
They believe in their Lord's signs, completing the receptive group introduced in 23:57 as a counterpart to those who avoid reminder.
They do not associate partners with their Lord, continuing the faithful response contrasted with refusal in the source.
They give while their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord, a direct form of fear that accompanies good action.
These believers hasten to good deeds, completing 23:57–60's portrait of fear and response.
The Messenger brings good news and warning, while most people turn away and do not hear; this directly stages reminder and refusal.
The hearers claim their hearts are covered and their ears stopped, making their distance from the offered message explicit.
If the audience turns away, the Prophet must say he warned them of a thunderbolt like those of Aad and Thamud; this gives the rejecter's consequence.
The man hears God's signs recited but persists proudly as if he had not heard, a precise instance of keeping reminder at a distance.
He takes the signs in mockery, and humiliating punishment is promised; this turns the refusal in 45:8 into consequence.
Hell awaits those described in 45:8–9, completing the refused signs' consequence and echoing the source's fire.
The one who makes desire his god is left astray despite knowledge and has hearing and heart sealed, a specific inward refusal of guidance.
They claim only worldly life exists and deny resurrection, the opposite of 87:17's better, abiding Hereafter.
The one who desires only the immediate life is promised Hell, making the source's warning against preferring dunya concrete.
The believer who strives for the Hereafter receives recompense, completing 17:18's choice and 87:17's enduring alternative.
When the Qur'an is recited, a hidden barrier separates the Prophet from those who deny the Hereafter, a concrete image of distance from reminder.
Their hearts have coverings and ears are stopped when the Lord alone is mentioned, explaining the barrier in 17:45 as refusal of remembrance.
When people mock God's signs, the Prophet must turn away until they change the subject; this is a concrete scene of disengaging from reminder.
Those deluded by worldly life are to be reminded by the Qur'an lest they be left to their deeds, joining reminder with the source's worldly preference.
Later generations neglect prayer and follow desires, a direct enactment of the source's lexical echo between avoidance and being far from prayer.
Those who repent and do right enter the Garden, completing 19:59's neglected prayer and desire with a path back to success.
The source explicitly gives junub as a state derived from ج ن ب because one stays away from prayer; this ayah uses جُنُبًا and restricts approach to prayer until purification.
The source's dictionary form junub is used for a state requiring purification here; the ritual cleansing offers a concrete lexical echo of the source's link to prayer.
The source labels ج ن ب's other sense as distance; الْجَارِ الْجُنُبِ can denote a distant or unrelated neighbor, a lexical echo, though this is social proximity rather than avoiding a reminder.
The source's ج ن ب distance sense echoes فَرَّطتُ فِي جَنبِ اللَّهِ, regret for neglecting what is due to God; this is a plausible figurative link to keeping reminder at a distance.
The one who stands in prayer fearing the Hereafter is set against the ignorant, joining the source's prayer, fear, and knowledge themes.
A heart opened to Islam and light is contrasted with hearts hardened against God's ذكر, directly portraying the source's two responses.
The revealed Qur'an makes the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver, then softens them to remembrance, a vivid scene of reminder received through fear.
The person shielding himself from the punishment with his face is asked whether he is like the secure; this makes the consequence of refusing reminder perceptible.
Earlier deniers were seized by punishment from where they did not expect, completing 39:24's image of exposure to punishment.
They taste humiliation in worldly life, while the afterlife punishment is greater, echoing the source's worldly/abiding contrast.
When Allah alone is mentioned, those who deny the Hereafter recoil, a concrete negative response to remembrance opposite 87:15.
Believers are told to fear Allah and consider what they sent ahead for tomorrow, linking fear to knowledge of the coming Day.
Those who forget Allah are made to forget themselves, a direct contrary to the source's reminder and remembrance theme.
If the Qur'an descended on a mountain it would humble and split from fear of Allah; this vividly shows the knowledge-born awe named in the source.
Those reminded of God's signs fall in prostration and glorify Him without arrogance, showing the response opposite to avoidance.
Their sides withdraw from beds as they call their Lord in fear and hope, completing 32:15's humble response with worship and fear.
The Book is sent down so the Prophet may warn by it and as a reminder for believers, explicitly linking the messenger's role and reminder.
People are told to follow what was sent down rather than other protectors and are said to remember little, a concrete reception choice.
Those who made religion amusement and forgot the meeting of that Day face its punishment, joining forgotten reminder to the source's rejected Hereafter.
Noah says a reminder from the Lord has come through a man to warn them so they may fear and receive mercy, a direct formulation of the source's scene.
Noah's people deny him, while he and those with him are saved and the deniers drowned; this makes the two responses consequential.
Hud repeats that a reminder has come to warn his people and make them fear, a second direct instance of the message the source describes.
The people challenge Hud to bring the threatened punishment and reject worship of Allah alone, showing their response to the warning.
Hud announces anger and punishment after their refusal in 7:70, completing the rejection scene.
Hud and the believers are saved while those who denied God's signs are cut off, completing the choice set in 7:69–71.
When those who fear God are touched by Satan, they remember and see clearly, directly joining fear with taking up reminder.
God's mercy is promised to those who repent after ignorance and set things right; this completes the humble audience contrast in 6:52–53.
A reminder from the Lord is described as healing for hearts, guidance, and mercy to believers, giving a specific account of how reminder benefits.
The Messenger is told to invite with wisdom and good instruction, specifying how the source's reminder is to be offered.
A group of jinn listens to the recited Qur'an attentively, then returns to warn its people, a scene of reminder received and passed on.
The jinn call the Qur'an a guide to truth, completing 46:29's listening with recognition of the message.
They urge their people to answer God's caller and believe so their sins may be forgiven, an explicit invitation to receive warning.
Whoever does not answer God's caller cannot escape God, completing the invitation and contrasting its acceptance with refusal.
The one who turned away from remembrance in 20:124 is raised blind and asks why, extending the consequence of refusing reminder.
The command describes people who turn away from God's remembrance and desire only worldly life, a near-exact pairing of the source section's avoider with its surah's later worldly-life contrast.
Whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Merciful is assigned a devil as companion, directly extending the source's image of keeping reminder at a distance.
The devils turn their companions from the way while they think they are guided; this completes 43:36's consequence for turning from remembrance.
The Qur'an is healing and mercy for believers but increases wrongdoers only in loss, giving a specific account of reminder's benefit or harm according to reception.
The Messenger complains that his people have treated the Qur'an as abandoned, an explicit form of the avoidant relation to reminder developed in the source.

The one guided by the Book benefits himself and the one who strays harms himself, while the Prophet is no guardian over them; this joins the source's benefit/harm distinction to its limit on the reminder-giver.
The Messenger says he cannot control harm or right guidance for his hearers, clarifying the source's contrast between offering a potentially beneficial reminder and controlling its effect.
If people turn away, their duty remains theirs and the Messenger's is clear conveyance; those who obey are guided, joining the source's avoider, receptive hearer, and preacher's boundary.
If people turn away, the Messenger's sole charge is clear delivery, a direct boundary on the reminder-giver's role in the source.
Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh that peace is for whoever follows guidance, directly linking their invitation to the source's root ه د ي and Pharaoh's choice.
They tell Pharaoh that punishment is for whoever denies and turns away, completing their invitation in 20:47 with the very response the source assigns to its avoider.
The people in Saqar are asked what brought them there; this opens the account in which the next ayah names abandoned prayer, the source's explicit lexical echo from ج ن ب.
The people in Saqar say they were not among those who prayed, directly illustrating the source's stated echo between avoidance from ج ن ب and distance from prayer.
They say they denied the Day of Judgment, a concrete form of rejecting the Hereafter against which the source's remembered, abiding Hereafter stands.
They say certainty came to them, completing 74:46's denial with the arrival of death before their regret.
Intercession will not benefit them, extending the source's harm/benefit distinction into the fate of those in Saqar.
The drinker's punishment brings death from every side but he does not die, a specific fire-scene parallel to 87:13's neither-death-nor-life condition.
The passage calls itself a reminder and says whoever wills may take a way to the Lord, a direct formulation of reminder and response.
This passage likewise calls itself a reminder and offers a way to the Lord to whoever wills, a repeated formulation of the source's voluntary reception.
The following ayah says human willing depends on God's will, completing 76:29's invitation to take the reminder's path.
The Qur'an is made easy for remembrance and the ayah asks who will take heed, echoing the source's beneficial reminder and the receptive listener.
This repeated refrain again asks whether anyone will take heed after the account of Aad, making it a distinct recurrence of the source's reminder-and-response pattern.
The same refrain follows the account of Thamud, another distinct recurrence of the question whether a listener will receive the reminder.
This refrain follows the account of Lut's people and asks who will take heed; Pharaoh's people come next in 54:41–42, adding a parallel warning scene to the source's Pharaoh connection.
The Qur'an is called a reminder for the God-conscious, joining the source's reminder to the fearful, receptive audience.
When the Qur'an is recited, people are told to listen and attend so they may receive mercy, specifying the accepting response contrasted in the source.
People are told to remember their Lord within themselves humbly and fearfully and not be heedless, joining the source's remembrance, fear, and avoidance themes.
When a surah is revealed, believers gain faith and rejoice; this depicts the positive response to revealed reminder that the source contrasts with avoidance.
The same revelation adds impurity to those with diseased hearts, completing 9:124's divided responses to the message.
The Qur'an guides to what is most upright and gives good news to believers, a concrete instance of the guidance root linked to the source's reminder.
Those who do not believe in the Hereafter face painful punishment, completing 17:9's contrast between the guided and those who reject the message.
The Prophet says he warns by revelation, but the deaf do not hear when warned; this restates the source's distinction between offering reminder and having it received.
The Qur'an is guidance and healing for believers while unbelievers remain deaf and blind to it, a concrete split response to the same revealed warning.
